newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan oil monopoly head indicted for impropriety.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan oil monopoly head indicted for impropriety.

text.p: The chairman of Taiwan's state-run oil monopoly was indicted on Friday on charges of public impropriety during his tenure as mayor of central Taichung city.
Chang Tzu-yuan, chairman of Chinese Petroleum Corp, denied the charges which relate to his tenure as mayor from 1985 to 1989.
"I am innocent," Chang Tzu-yuan told reporters.
Chang was indicted on charges stemming from allegations of misconduct in Taichung's 1986 re-zoning of local property, a Taichung district prosecutor told reporters.

A spokesman for the economics ministry said the charges, unrelated to Chinese Petroleum, carried a maximum six-year prison term and the ministry would decide whether to suspend Chang after receiving a formal written notice from prosecutors.
Chang said he was surprised by the indictment, but would accept any punishment from the ministry.
"This indictment came out of nowhere and is very unusual," Chang said. "But I will accept any economics ministry decision."
It is up to the ministry what steps are taken next.
The indictment was the latest in a string of blows to hit Taiwan's oil giant.

Company president Chen Kuo-young resigned on November 19 to take responsibility for a series of explosions, fires and oil spills that cost the company millions of dollars in compensation claims and fines in 1996.

Chinese Petroleum, which reported a huge budget deficit in November, finally saw its fiscal 1996-97 budget adopted by parliament on Thursday after months of political footdragging over its proposed privatisation and other contentious issues.
The budget stalemate and popular opposition have prevented Chinese Petroleum from carrying through oil price increases that would enable it to balance its budget.

Parliament cut the monopoly's budget for key overseas expansion programmes in Indonesia and Vietnam and cancelled its participation in a consortium planning to build a power station in northern Taiwan.
Chang has vowed to stay on at Chinese Petroleum despite mounting criticism of his stewardship from lawmakers, government officials and Taiwan's media.
